extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent attorneys, and judges considering § 101 patent-eligibility challenges (especially for computer-implemented inventions)
extracted.subtask_description: Applying the two-step Alice framework to determine whether asserted patent claims are directed to patent-ineligible subject matter (abstract ideas) and, if so, whether claim elements supply an inventive concept that renders them patent-eligible. Emphasis on computer-implemented inventions and pleadings-stage dismissals under Rule 12(b)(6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice two-step test
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the Supreme Court's two-step Alice framework: (1) determine whether a claim is directed to a patent-ineligible concept like an abstract idea; (2) if so, determine whether the claim recites elements sufficient to transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (i.e., contains an 'inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted formulation: 'Under step one of the Alice test, we review whether a claim is directed to a patent-ineligible concept like an abstract idea. ... At step two, we review whether the claim recites elements sufficient to transform it into a patent-eligible application.' (Alice, 573 U.S. 208). Use this two-step framework as the controlling inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice Step One — 'directed to' inquiry (character of the claims as a whole)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'directed to' inquiry looks to the character of the claims as a whole and does more than simply ask whether the claims involve a patent-ineligible concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the claimed advance over the prior art (the focus of the claimed advance). Avoid characterizing claims at too high a level of generality untethered from claim language. See Enfish (look to character of the claims as a whole), Affinity Labs, and Free Stream Media guidance about examining limitations that describe the claimed advance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the claimed advance over the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: In computer-related cases, determine whether the focus of the claimed advance is an improvement in computer technology (which can be non-abstract) rather than the mere use of computers to perform an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claims 'focus on a specific means or method that improves the relevant technology' they may be non-abstract (McRO). Otherwise, a claim that merely uses computers to obtain/manipulate/display data is likely directed to an abstract idea (Electric Power Group, Affinity Labs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid importing specification details into claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the specification but do not import unclaimed details from the specification into the claims when performing the Alice analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ChargePoint and Phillips: specification evidence may inform the inquiry, but courts must avoid importing specification concepts into the claims themselves. Claimed limitations matter; unclaimed technical details in the spec do not save otherwise abstract claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-level functional claiming is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming a functionally-stated capability 'at a high level of generality' does not save a claim from abstraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional limitations that merely recite goals or outcomes without concrete means (e.g., 'achieving that stated goal' recited only functionally) fail to transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstractness of data-manipulation: obtaining/manipulating/displaying data
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps of obtaining, manipulating, and displaying data — particularly when claimed at a high level of generality — are abstract concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: converting data, creating virtual views from an existing dataset, and similar data-manipulation steps are treated as abstract (Electric Power Group, Hawk Tech Systems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific example — converting information between formats is abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Converting information from one format to another is an abstract idea and does not, by itself, render a claim patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As stated in Hawk: 'converting information from one format to another . . . is an abstract idea.' Use such examples to assess whether claimed steps are merely abstract data transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice Step Two — 'significantly more' / inventive concept requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: At step two, the claim elements, individually and as an ordered combination, must supply 'significantly more' than the abstract idea — an 'inventive concept' that transforms the claim into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask 'What else is there in the claims before us?' (Mayo). Mere recitation of the abstract idea plus conventional computer implementation is insufficient (Alice, Mayo, BSG Tech).

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine, conventional, well-understood elements cannot supply the inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim elements or combinations that are routine, conventional, or well-known in the art do not transform an abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the intrinsic record (or properly pleaded facts) shows the technology is conventional (e.g., generic computer components), the claim fails at step two (BSG Tech, Int'l Bus. Machs. v. Zillow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer components performing abstract ideas insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely reciting conventional computer components or a generic computer performing the abstract idea does not provide an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that 'merely recit[e] an abstract idea performed on a set of generic computer components' are not saved at Alice step two (Two-Way Media; BASCOM guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Real-time/on-demand operation alone is not a saving inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming that an operation occurs 'on demand', 'in real time', or 'on the fly' does not by itself render the claim patent-eligible absent a concrete application or unconventional technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affinity Labs and Electric Power Group illustrate that 'real time' or 'customized user interface' language without a concrete technological improvement is insufficient. The same logic applies to 'on-demand' virtual view creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegations of inventive concept may require factual support at pleading stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a limitation supplies an inventive concept can involve underlying factual questions; patentees who adequately allege factual bases for inventive concepts can survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Berkheimer and Aatrix: at the motion-to-dismiss stage, well-pleaded factual allegations that claim elements are unconventional may prevent dismissal. Conclusory allegations or allegations 'wholly divorced' from the claims/specification are insufficient (Cellspin, Simio).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6) in § 101 context
rubrics_metrics.description: A complaint must allege 'enough facts to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face' to survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion; § 101 issues may be resolved on the pleadings when undisputed facts require ineligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Twombly/Iqbal plausibility standard. Federal Circuit reviews grant of 12(b)(6) de novo (Endo Pharms. citation). If intrinsic record and complaint facts are undisputed and show conventionality/abstractness, dismissal is appropriate (SAP Am. v. InvestPic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative-claim treatment in § 101 analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be treated as representative for the § 101 inquiry if the patentee makes no meaningful argument for distinctive significance of limitations not present in the representative claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Berkheimer allows grouping claims and using representative claims where no meaningful differences are argued; parties may sort asserted claims into groups for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate claims in light of the intrinsic record
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the claims in light of the specification and the intrinsic record to determine whether the claimed advance is indeed technical and unconventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intrinsic evidence can show that an asserted 'innovation' was known in the art (undermining eligibility). But courts should not import unclaimed details from the spec into the claims; rather, use the spec to inform claim focus and conventionality.
